title: Hidden dependencies create technical debt
lead: An innocent upstream change can alter ML behavior without changing the model.
bullets: Hidden coupling: features depend on sources owned by other teams.
Pipeline complexity: parallel preparation paths can diverge.
Versioning gaps: a model artifact alone cannot reproduce a decision.
Context matters: architecture decisions depend on requirements and constraints.
example: CRM changes its engagement export for another purpose; both training and production can inherit the change.
takeaway: Make data dependencies as reviewable as code dependencies.

title: Make the feature contract explicit
lead: A contract records meaning and ownership as well as structural schema.
bullets: Semantics: define what the feature actually measures.
Time: specify window, cutoff, and joins consistently.
Validity: define types, ranges, freshness, and missingness.
Ownership: review upstream changes with affected consumers.
example: engagement_7d means app logins during seven days ending at the scoring cutoff; missing must not silently become zero.
takeaway: Schema checks alone cannot detect every change in meaning.

title: Separate responsibilities where change happens
lead: Clear interfaces let different concerns evolve without unnecessary relearning.
bullets: Single responsibility: identify each module’s reason to change.
Interfaces: specify data and behavior at each boundary.
Dependency injection: provide implementations through explicit contracts.
Deployment: logical modules do not automatically require separate services.
example: A connector fix changes preparation; a contact-frequency rule changes campaign policy; a new M2 changes inference.
takeaway: Separate concerns first; choose deployment units from the actual trade-offs.

title: Pipeline pattern: order the responsibilities
lead: Make preparation and validation steps explicit and testable.
bullets: Explicit stages clarify transformations and dependencies.
Stage contracts make intermediate data understandable.
Tests cover local behavior and end-to-end compatibility.
Failure handling prevents a partial result from masquerading as a complete batch.
example: Validate CRM records before computing engagement_7d and invoking M1.
takeaway: Use structure to expose the dependency, not to hide it in orchestration code.

title: Strategy pattern: replace one implementation
lead: A stable interface separates the client from a specific implementation choice.
bullets: Stable interface: the client relies on a contract, not a specific class.
Alternative implementations can be supplied through that interface.
Compatibility still includes meaning, not only types.
Evaluation and release approval still apply when behavior changes.
example: Replace a feature-preparation implementation behind a stable interface; verify equivalent semantics before scoring.
takeaway: Interchangeability in code is not equivalence in predictive behavior.

title: Observer pattern: notify, then investigate
lead: A change notification decouples the signal producer from interested responders.
bullets: Subject: emits a meaningful change event.
Subscribers: receive notifications without tightly coupling the producer.
Context: include cohort, reference, and evidence links.
Authority: receiving a notification does not grant release privileges.
example: A missingness event notifies data and operations owners; it does not instruct the registry to promote M2.
takeaway: A useful notification requests attention and preserves the decision boundary.

title: Version the system, not only the model
lead: A prediction depends on a compatible set of data meaning, code, model, and configuration.
bullets: Data meaning: record source and feature definitions.
Code: identify preparation and scoring revisions.
Model: identify artifact, runtime, and configuration.
Outputs: connect the compatible set to score and decision records.
example: M1 alone cannot explain Ana’s score if a CRM migration changed the meaning of its engagement input.
takeaway: Co-versioning connects system and model lifecycles.

title: Modules or services? Make the trade-off
lead: Independent deployment is useful only when it justifies its operating cost.
bullets: Modules can provide strong logical boundaries with simpler operation.
Services can support independent change and scaling.
Distribution adds failure modes and version coordination.
Evidence and requirements should drive the choice.
example: Separate preparation from policy logically; deploy them independently only when the bank’s needs justify it.
takeaway: There is no universal best ML architecture.
